title: Netaji Ka Chasmaa
author: Swayam Prakash
tagline: A lame, mocking-laughed-at vendor keeps placing a pair of glasses on Netaji’s statue — and children finish his work.

overview.intro: Swayam Prakash’s "Netaji Ka Chasmaa" ("Netaji’s Spectacles") is a quiet story about everyday patriotism. Haldar Sahib, a travelling employee, notices that the marble bust of Subhas Chandra Bose in a small town’s square wears real spectacles that keep changing. A paan seller explains that an elderly, lame glasses-seller known as Captain keeps putting a frame on the statue, because it seems wrong to him that Netaji should sit bare-faced. The townspeople laugh at Captain as a madman; Haldar is moved. When Captain dies and the statue stands bare, a small pair of reed spectacles appears — left, it seems, by children.

learningOutcomes: Retell how Captain comes to place glasses on Netaji’s statue and what happens after his death.
Explain the reactions of the townspeople and the paan seller, and how Haldar’s view differs.
Comment on the significance of the reed spectacles placed by the children.
Discuss the story’s message about the patriotism of ordinary people.

blocks.text: Haldar Sahib passes through the town regularly on work, and on one visit he notices the marble bust of Netaji in the square. It is a good likeness except for one detail: Master Motilal, the drawing teacher who made it, did not carve a pair of spectacles, and everyone knows Netaji wore them. What Haldar then notices is stranger — the statue is wearing real glasses, and on the next visit the frame is different.

The story is built on this small, persistent oddity. A statue that keeps changing its spectacles should be a mystery; instead it turns out to be an act of devotion repeated by one unremarkable man. Swayam Prakash uses Haldar’s curiosity as the reader’s own, holding back the explanation so that the answer arrives as a gentle surprise rather than a lesson.

learn.title: Captain: the man who could not bear an unclad statue

items.meaning: An elderly, lame street vendor of spectacles who repeatedly places a frame on Netaji’s statue.
A travelling company employee whose curiosity about the statue grows into respect for Captain.
A comic, dismissive townsman who reports Captain’s habit and mocks him as mad.
The local drawing teacher who made the statue and omitted a carved pair of spectacles.
Unidentified children who leave a small pair of reed spectacles after Captain’s death.

blocks.text: The paan seller’s explanation gives the story its human centre. Captain is poor, old and lame, and he earns his living by selling glasses from his stock. When a customer needs the very frame sitting on the statue, Captain simply swaps it for another — so the statue’s spectacles change not from fancy but from the everyday economics of a street vendor combined with an unshakeable sense that Netaji should not be left without them.

items: The paan seller mocks Captain and tells Haldar that the old man is mad.
He adds, dismissively, that Captain was never even a soldier.
Haldar, however, is moved by the sincerity of the gesture rather than amused by it.
Over about two years Haldar keeps returning and keeps finding different glasses on the statue.
One day the statue has no glasses at all, and Haldar learns that Captain has died.

blocks.text: The town’s mockery is the story’s real target. Captain’s devotion is judged by the wrong standards — by whether he was a soldier, by whether it is "sensible", by whether an old vendor has any business feeling what he feels. Haldar, the outsider, judges it by the only standard that matters: sincerity. The contrast between the laughing insider and the moved outsider is what gives the story its satirical edge.

blocks.caption: The statue through Haldar’s visits
rows: Devotion sustained, funded by his trade
A public loss that the town barely notices
A small pair of reed spectacles
Children have taken up the gesture

blocks.text: On his last visit Haldar expects the statue to stand bare. Instead a small pair of spectacles made of reeds sits on its face, and he understands that children have taken over Captain’s quiet work. The detail is deliberately modest — reeds, not real frames — and it is exactly that modesty that makes the ending moving. The story closes with Haldar stopping to salute, his eyes filling with tears.

learn.title: Themes: ordinary patriotism and the dignity of small acts

items.text: Captain swaps the statue’s frame when a customer needs it.
items.note: Devotion and livelihood are woven together; the gesture costs him a sale but never stops.

items.text: The paan seller says Captain was never a soldier.
items.note: The town measures patriotism by rank and service record, and so misses it entirely in front of them.

items.text: Children leave reed spectacles after Captain’s death.
items.note: The gesture survives its originator, which is the story’s quiet hope.

blocks.text: The themes gather around one idea: patriotism is not confined to heroism or official recognition. It can be a lame vendor’s stubborn courtesy toward a statue. The story also values memory and continuity — the public symbol is kept lovingly by the least powerful members of the town, and the impulse passes to a new generation. Finally, it gently satirises a public that mocks sincerity while never troubling itself to do anything.

This story usually yields a short note on its central idea or a character sketch of Captain. In either, keep the reed spectacles in reserve as your closing image, since they carry the story’s whole argument about continuity and ordinary devotion. Be ready to explain why the town’s mockery is the real subject of the satire, and why Haldar, the outsider, sees more clearly than the townspeople.

items: Explain the practical reason the glasses keep changing — Captain sells them for a living.
Contrast the paan seller’s mockery with Haldar’s respect to draw out the satire.
Use the reed spectacles to show that the gesture outlives the man who began it.

keyPoints: Master Motilal made the marble bust of Netaji but did not carve spectacles, though Netaji wore them.
Captain, an elderly lame vendor, places real glasses on the statue because it seems wrong to leave him bare-faced.
Captain sells spectacles for a living, so he swaps frames when a customer needs one — the glasses keep changing.
The paan seller mocks Captain as mad and sneers that he was never a soldier.
Haldar, the travelling outsider, is moved rather than amused, and judges by sincerity rather than rank.
Over about two years the statue’s glasses keep changing, showing the devotion is sustained, not occasional.
After Captain’s dies the statue stands bare — a loss the town barely registers.
A small pair of reed spectacles then appears, left by children: the gesture survives, and Haldar salutes with tears.
examFocus: Central idea: patriotism lives in small, sincere acts by ordinary people and needs no rank or recognition.
Character sketch of Captain: poor, old, lame, mocked — and quietly devoted to a public symbol.
Significance of the reed spectacles: children continue the work, so devotion passes to a new generation.

questions.prompt: Why does the statue of Netaji in the town square lack carved spectacles?
options: The drawing teacher who made it did not carve them
Netaji is shown without them by custom
questions.answer: The drawing teacher who made it did not carve them
questions.explanation: Master Motilal, the local drawing teacher who made the marble bust, omitted a carved pair of spectacles — an omission that gives Captain his opportunity.
questions.commonMistake: The glasses are not missing because of damage or theft; they were never carved.

questions.prompt: Who keeps placing glasses on the statue?
questions.explanation: Captain, a poor elderly street vendor who sells spectacles and walks with a limp, repeatedly places a frame on the statue because it seems wrong to him that Netaji should be without glasses.
questions.commonMistake: It is neither the sculptor nor an official but a poor vendor.

questions.prompt: Why do the glasses on the statue keep changing?
options: Captain swaps in another frame when a customer needs the one on the statue
questions.answer: Captain swaps in another frame when a customer needs the one on the statue
questions.explanation: Because Captain earns his living selling spectacles, when a customer wants the particular frame on the statue he exchanges it for another from his stock — so the frame visibly changes over time.
questions.commonMistake: The changes come from Captain’s trade, not from vandalism or donations.

questions.prompt: How does the paan seller describe Captain?
options: As a madman who was never even a soldier
questions.answer: As a madman who was never even a soldier
questions.explanation: The paan seller dismisses Captain as mad and sneers that he was never a soldier, using both mockery and the argument from rank to belittle the gesture.
questions.commonMistake: The townsman’s contempt is the story’s satirical target, not its judgement of Captain.

questions.prompt: How does Haldar Sahib react to Captain’s habit?
questions.answer: He is moved rather than amused, and comes to respect the sincerity of the gesture even as the town mocks it.
questions.explanation: As an outsider, Haldar judges the act by its sincerity rather than by rank or convention, and his feeling deepens over the years of passing through the town.
questions.commonMistake: Haldar does not join the mockery; his difference from the townspeople is the point.

questions.prompt: What does Haldar find on the statue after Captain’s death?
questions.answer: After a bare interval, he finds a small pair of spectacles made of reeds, apparently placed there by children.
questions.explanation: On the visit after learning of Captain’s death, Haldar expects the statue to remain bare; instead reed spectacles sit on its face, showing that the gesture has been taken up by the town’s children.
questions.commonMistake: Two stages matter — first bare, then the reed spectacles by children.

questions.prompt: Explain why the story presents the townspeople’s reaction to Captain as its real satire.
questions.answer: The townspeople judge Captain by the wrong measures: the paan seller calls him mad and sneers that he was never a soldier, as if patriotism were the property of rank and official service. In doing so the town mocks the very devotion it ought to recognise, while doing nothing itself for the public symbol. Haldar, the outsider, reads the act correctly because he judges it by sincerity alone. The satire therefore falls not on Captain but on a comfortable public that laughs at sincerity and never troubling itself to act.
questions.explanation: A strong answer contrasts the two standards — rank and convention against sincerity — and shows that the mockery exposes the town’s own spiritual laziness rather than Captain’s folly.
questions.commonMistake: Do not treat the mockery as comic relief; it is the object of the story’s critique.

questions.prompt: What do the reed spectacles at the end symbolise?
questions.answer: They show that Captain’s quiet devotion has been taken up by a new generation, so the gesture survives the man who began it.
questions.explanation: The modest reed frame, plainly left by children, indicates continuity: ordinary patriotism passes from an old vendor to the town’s children, which is the story’s closing hope.
questions.commonMistake: The reeds matter as much for who left them as for what they are.

questions.prompt: Trace Haldar’s encounters with the statue and show what the story says about ordinary people’s patriotism.
questions.answer: Haldar Sahib, a traveller passing through the town, first notices that the marble bust of Netaji wears real spectacles though none were carved. On later visits the frame is always different, and a paan seller explains that Captain, an elderly lame vendor, places them there because it seems wrong that Netaji should go without. The paan seller mocks Captain as mad and says he was never a soldier, but Haldar is moved by the sincerity of the act. Over about two years the glasses keep changing, since Captain sells them for a living and swaps frames when a customer needs one. After Captain’s death the statue stands bare, and then a small pair of reed spectacles appears, left by children. Haldar stops to salute, in tears. The story argues that patriotism is not confined to heroism or rank: a poor vendor’s stubborn courtesy toward a public statue is patriotism in its truest, most everyday form, and it can pass from one generation to the next.
questions.explanation: The sequence — first frame, changing frames, bare statue, reed spectacles, salute — carries the argument. Name the theme of ordinary, unshowy patriotism explicitly in the conclusion.
questions.commonMistake: Do not stop at the plot; the question asks what the story says, so interpret each stage.

questions.prompt: Captain was mocked for his gesture. Do you think such acts of everyday patriotism still matter? Discuss.
questions.answer: Captain’s act mattered precisely because it was small, persistent and asked nothing in return: it honoured a public symbol when no one else would, and it cost him real livelihood. The story suggests that a society is held together by such uncelebrated gestures far more than by occasional grand displays, and the reed spectacles prove the point by showing the impulse spreading to children. Today, when public spaces and symbols are often neglected, an equivalent act might be caring for a memorial, keeping a public place clean or teaching a child the meaning of a national day. What the story asks us to value is sincerity rather than scale.
questions.explanation: Take a clear position, ground it in the text (Captain’s persistence, the mockery, the children’s reeds), then extend it to a modern equivalent so the answer reasons rather than repeats.
questions.commonMistake: Do not argue only that "it is nice"; show why small, sustained acts matter to a society’s memory.
